title: How To Handle Entitled Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin defines entitled students as charming or talented students who believe the normal rules do not apply to them, often because adults have let them slide out of fear or admiration. He argues this deference is deeply harmful, setting students up to fail later in life when they encounter environments that demand skill, discipline, and hard work. The article offers five guidelines for correcting this pattern: committing to equal treatment from day one, avoiding personal explanations or special talks, resisting a student's charm offensives, following through boldly without hesitation, and still greeting the student warmly afterward to show there's no grudge. He frames differential treatment based on personality or talent as a form of discrimination that denies students the habits and humility needed to succeed. The piece closes by describing entitled students' eventual reckoning when the special treatment inevitably ends.
points: Entitled students are given a 'free pass' by adults out of fear or fondness, which sets them up to struggle badly once that treatment ends.
Committing to equal treatment from the very start of the year is far easier than trying to reassert boundaries later.
Teachers should avoid personal explanations, special talks, or responding to charm offensives that entitled students use to test boundaries.
Following through on consequences boldly and without hesitation is essential, even when a student reacts with anger or charm.
Treating some students differently because of personality or talent denies them the habits of hard work, responsibility, and humility needed later in life.
quotes: Charming, stylish, and often athletically talented, entitled students believe they’re special and not subject to the same boundaries and expectations as others.
It’s terrible for them. One day the piper will come calling requiring skill, discipline, and hard work and they’ll have none of these. In the end, they pay. And they pay dearly.
Promise to follow through for all students from day one, damn the torpedoes, and everything becomes much easier.
They’ll act angry for awhile and when that doesn’t work they’ll lay on the charm. You must resist. Smiling is fine, but don’t say much when they begin to justify, cajole, and plead.
Treating some students differently because of their personality or athletic ability or any other reason is discriminatory. Plain and simple.
So many of these students find out too late that their entitlement doesn’t last beyond eighth grade or high school, and they can’t handle it. They’re unprepared for it.
